[audio mp3="https://thebluetree.pl/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Q1-How-to-Make-Stress-Your-Friend.mp3"][/audio]

 Why do most people automatically assume that stress is always bad for their health?
[/et_pb_text][et_pb_toggle title="TRANSCRIPT" open_toggle_text_color="#663366" open_toggle_background_color="#ffffff" closed_toggle_background_color="rgba(102,51,102,0.44)" icon_color="#ffffff" use_icon_font_size="on" icon_font_size="30px" open_icon_color="#ffffff" open_use_icon_font_size="on" open_icon_font_size="30px" admin_label="TRANSCRIPT 1" _builder_version="4.27.4" title_text_color="#663366" title_font="Roboto|700||||on|||" title_font_size="24px" title_letter_spacing="2px" body_font="Roboto Slab|300|||||||" body_text_color="#660000" body_font_size="16px" global_colors_info="{}"]

For decades, the message from health experts has been clear — stress kills. That idea has been repeated so often that most people accept it without question. When you constantly hear that stress causes heart disease and burnout, it's natural to see every stressful moment as a threat. I think the problem is that this oversimplified message ignores important nuances about how the body actually responds to different types of pressure.

[/et_pb_toggle][et_pb_text admin_label="AUDIO AND QUESTION 2" _builder_version="4.27.9" _module_preset="default" text_font="|300|||||||" global_colors_info="{}"]

[audio mp3="https://thebluetree.pl/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Q2-How-to-Make-Stress-Your-Friend.mp3"][/audio]

 What role does mindset play in how people handle pressure and difficult situations?
[/et_pb_text][et_pb_toggle title="TRANSCRIPT" open_toggle_text_color="#663366" open_toggle_background_color="#ffffff" closed_toggle_background_color="rgba(102,51,102,0.44)" icon_color="#ffffff" use_icon_font_size="on" icon_font_size="30px" open_icon_color="#ffffff" open_use_icon_font_size="on" open_icon_font_size="30px" admin_label="TRANSCRIPT 2" _builder_version="4.27.4" title_text_color="#663366" title_font="Roboto|700||||on|||" title_font_size="24px" title_letter_spacing="2px" body_font="Roboto Slab|300|||||||" body_text_color="#660000" body_font_size="16px" global_colors_info="{}"]

Mindset is probably more powerful than most people realise. Two people can face the same challenge and respond completely differently depending on how they interpret the situation. If you see pressure as a sign that something matters to you, it becomes energising rather than paralysing. I've always believed that difficulties are easier to handle when you view them as opportunities to grow rather than threats to survive.

[/et_pb_toggle][et_pb_text admin_label="AUDIO AND QUESTION 3" _builder_version="4.27.4" _module_preset="default" text_font="|300|||||||" global_colors_info="{}"]

[audio mp3="https://thebluetree.pl/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Q3-How-to-Make-Stress-Your-Friend.mp3"][/audio]

 How do you typically react when you feel stressed — do you withdraw, seek support, or try to push through on your own?
[/et_pb_text][et_pb_toggle title="TRANSCRIPT" open_toggle_text_color="#663366" open_toggle_background_color="#ffffff" closed_toggle_background_color="rgba(102,51,102,0.44)" icon_color="#ffffff" use_icon_font_size="on" icon_font_size="30px" open_icon_color="#ffffff" open_use_icon_font_size="on" open_icon_font_size="30px" admin_label="TRANSCRIPT 3" _builder_version="4.27.4" title_text_color="#663366" title_font="Roboto|700||||on|||" title_font_size="24px" title_letter_spacing="2px" body_font="Roboto Slab|300|||||||" body_text_color="#660000" body_font_size="16px" global_colors_info="{}"]

I think people can develop wisdom without much personal experience if they actively learn from others. Reading is one way — books let you explore situations you haven't faced yourself. But observing how other people handle problems can also teach you a lot. The key is thinking critically about what you learn rather than just absorbing information passively. That kind of reflection can build real understanding surprisingly quickly.

2 5:12 How do we tend to interpret these changes??We usually interpret them as anxiety or as signs that we are not coping with the pressure.

6 6:04 What is a typical stress response??Your heart rate goes up and your blood vessels constrict.
7 6:12 What toll could chronic stress have on you??It can lead to cardiovascular disease because the body stays in this constricted state too often.
8 6:32 How did the group of participants who viewed stress as helpful respond physically??Their blood vessels stayed relaxed, even though their hearts were still pounding — a much healthier cardiovascular profile.
9 6:52 What does the new science of stress reveal??That how you think about stress really matters and can change how your body responds to it.
10 7:00 How did her goal change as a psychologist??She no longer wants to get rid of people's stress — she wants to make them better at handling it.
11 7:08 What could have saved the lives of those who experience lots of stress??Learning to see their stress response as the body helping them rise to a challenge.
12 7:28 On what condition does our stress response become healthier??When we view stress as helpful rather than harmful — when the body "believes" us, the response itself changes.

11 10:36 Under what circumstances do we release more oxytocin??When we reach out to others under stress — either to seek support or to help someone else.
12 10:49 What is a built-in mechanism we have for stress resilience??Human connection — reaching out to others.

Alita: You look surprisingly relaxed for someone who had three big presentations this week. How do you handle stress so well these days?

Pete: Honestly, I've changed my mind about it. I used to think stress was something I had to get rid of, but I listened to a podcast that completely shifted my perspective.

Alita: That sounds intriguing. What did it say?

Pete: Well, the speaker made a kind of confession — for years she had been telling people that stress does more harm than good and even increases the risk of a disease. But then a big study made her rethink her whole approach.

Alita: Really? So stress isn't always the enemy?

Pete: Not exactly. The study showed that people who experience stress but don't believe it's harmful actually have the lowest risk of dying. The belief itself matters more than the stress.

Alita: That's a fascinating finding. So when my heart starts pounding before a meeting, I shouldn't freak out about it?

Pete: Exactly. You can view it as your body preparing you to rise to the challenge. Apparently, when you see your stress response as helpful, even your blood vessels stay more relaxed.

Alita: That's quite a profound idea. So what do you actually do differently now?

Pete: Two things. First, I try to feel energised by the pressure instead of anxious. And second — this surprised me — I reach out to others more often. The speaker said connection is a built-in mechanism for resilience.

Alita: Interesting. So instead of bottling it up, you talk to someone.

Pete: Right. And helping others when you're stressed seems to work even better than just seeking support for yourself.

Alita: That's a really compassionate way to look at it. Maybe the goal isn't a stress-free life, but learning to face challenges without fearing them.

Pete: Exactly. Chase meaning instead of trying to avoid discomfort — that's the takeaway I keep coming back to.
